source.title: Binary Sparse Coding for Interpretability
source.authors: Lucia Quirke; Stepan Shabalin; Nora Belrose

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse coding to SmolLM2 language models and reports results about whether sparse-coder features are interpretable or useful for representing concepts. It does not reproduce the toy-model superposition setup or measure superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own sparse-coder feature interpretability, sparse-probing, firing-frequency, and feature-ablation results. It does not measure feature overlap, orthogonality, feature count versus network dimensions, or neuron-to-feature distribution. Cited claims and results from other papers are not treated as findings here. Figure-based aggregate results are recorded as figure-only where the text gives a qualitative description but no numerical values.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It proposes binary sparse coders and compares them with continuous TopK skip-transcoders and SAEs on SmolLM2, using auto-interp F1, sparse probing, loss and firing rates. SAE features serve as the tool throughout. The paper has no neuron baseline, no ground-truth features, and no measure of feature overlap, spread across neurons, completeness, stability or dimensionality. Its own results are the performance of its method against other coders. Its broader point that 'polysemanticity may be ineliminable' is a hypothesis the authors 'suspect but cannot prove'. So no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Binarisation improves unweighted interpretability but raises reconstruction error and loss and adds uninterpretable ultra-high-frequency features. Frequency-weighted, continuous coders score slightly better on SmolLM2-135M. The authors call the primary result negative and do not recommend binary coders for most purposes. They suggest, but cannot prove, that polysemanticity is ineliminable.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains binary and continuous sparse autoencoders/transcoders on SmolLM2 activations and evaluates interpretability, probing, and patched-model performance. It does not use the original toy-network superposition setup or test overlap geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with binary versus continuous coding, frequency weighting, layer, k, finetuning, and model size; the SmolLM2-1.7B table is a single-seed run.

fits_no_version.finding: Binarising activations raises unweighted interpretability but creates uninterpretable ultra-high-frequency features. Frequency-weighted scores for continuous coders end up slightly better on the 135M sweep. The authors read this as polysemanticity being displaced, not removed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Constraining sparse-coder activations (e.g. binarisation) relocates polysemanticity into high-frequency dictionary features rather than eliminating it.

fits_no_version.finding: Zero-ablating feature bins of equal firing count gives nearly equal loss increases across most fuzzing-F1 bins, except the two most interpretable bins.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dictionary-feature interpretability scores are largely unrelated to causal importance, except at the high-interpretability extreme.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2025 (39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems)
record.problems: The study focuses on a sample of one model training corpus; the authors note that some sparse coders have many dead neurons and results may differ at greater widths. Interpretability is evaluated with Llama 3.1 auto-interpretability and can overestimate feature interpretability, as shown by a case-study counterexample. SmolLM2-1.7B results are a single-seed run. The study does not measure superposition geometry or compare recovered features with ground truth.
record.rows_left_out: No reported qualifying result was left out. Values in Figures 1 and 8 that concern reconstruction loss or feature-ablation loss without measuring the V4 feature-recovery claim were not included as V4 rows; figure-only values are not transcribed as numbers.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep, geometry or transition.
No test of capacity competition or of dedicated dimensions for important features.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
No measurement of features spread across neurons, and no neuron or ground-truth baseline for SAE feature recovery. Only coder-vs-coder comparisons.
No test of completeness, stability across seeds or widths, or canonicality of SAE features.
No comparison of 1-D vs multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'supports' and 'limits_scope' labels should be dropped. Every row compares the study's own binary coders with continuous coders and has no baseline bearing on whether features are recovered from the LLM. The 1.7B weighted scores favouring binary (r25, r27) come from a single seed and run opposite to the 135M sweep. The original source, Toy Models, is cited only as background on polysemanticity.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, sparse-feature-versus-dimension sweep, overlap geometry, orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometry are tested.
The study does not test whether feature competition for capacity causes neuron polysemanticity, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
It does not test causes of neuron polysemanticity independent of capacity pressure.
The study evaluates sparse-coder features in SmolLM2, but does not measure how many neurons each feature is spread across or compare SAE features against a ground-truth feature set.
It does not establish completeness, stability across conditions, or canonical status of SAE features. Imperfect interpretability scores and counterexamples do not directly test those properties.
No comparison of one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features is made.

rows.note: Authors say interpretability and causal influence have no relation across most bins, with a positive relation at the extremes.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SmolLM2-135M sparse-coder feature evaluations and the reported SmolLM2-1.7B single-seed evaluation
reader_labels.reason: Sparse coders yield features with measurable interpretability and concept-probing performance; the binary 1.7B coder has higher scores on all four reported interpretability metrics, and Figure 2 says binary matches or outperforms continuous coders across shown 135M settings (r1-r29).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Frequency-weighted scores, sparse-probing conditions, and individual feature inspection
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports that binary coders are often worse on frequency-weighted interpretability, probing results vary by layer and finetuning, and a feature with perfect scores has counterexamples; ultra-high-frequency binary features are often poorly interpretable (r2,r5,r7,r10,r12,r15,r17,r20,r30-r33).
